title: Key prefixing
description: The simplest isolation: every key is namespaced as tenant_id + ':' + key, so two tenants can both own 'settings' without colliding. It costs nothing at read time and works on any key-value store. The discipline is in the client library — one raw unprefixed write bypasses the whole scheme, so prefixing belongs in the access layer, not in application code.
mechanism: Access layer prepends the authenticated tenant id to every key before touching storage. Key scans and deletes are scoped by prefix range. Never let callers supply their own prefix.
algo: O(1) prefix concatenation per op. Prefix scans are range scans over the keyspace: O(matches).

title: Silo vs pool tenancy models
description: Tenant isolation comes in three flavors: silo (a whole database per tenant — maximum isolation, maximum cost), pool (everyone shares tables with a tenant_id column — cheapest, needs the most discipline), and bridge (shared database, separate schemas). Vector and search platforms usually run pool for metadata with silo available as a paid tier for regulated customers.
mechanism: Silo: provision per-tenant infrastructure. Pool: add tenant_id to every table/index and enforce it in the query planner. Bridge: per-tenant schemas in one database with search_path switching.
algo: Pool adds one equality predicate per query (index-friendly). Silo multiplies infra cost by tenant count; pool is O(1) infra per tenant.
demo:
# pool model: one table, tenant_id on every row, planner enforces it
rows = [
    {'tenant': 'acme', 'doc': 'acme-secret-plan'},
    {'tenant': 'globex', 'doc': 'globex-prices'},
    {'tenant': 'acme', 'doc': 'acme-notes'},
]

def query(tenant):
    return [r['doc'] for r in rows if r['tenant'] == tenant]  # predicate enforced

print('acme  :', query('acme'))
print('globex:', query('globex'))
print('no tenant predicate -> leak; the planner must add it, not the app')

title: ACLs on namespaces
description: Access-control lists attach permissions to namespaces: who can read, write, or administer each tenant's data. Checks happen on every operation against the authenticated identity — not just at login. The classic failure is checking at the front door and then passing raw internal ids around, letting one tenant guess another's resource ids.
mechanism: On each request: authenticate -> resolve tenant -> load ACL for the target namespace -> require the needed permission bit. Deny by default; log denials. Use capability-style unguessable ids so enumeration is useless even if a check is missed.
algo: ACL check is O(1) hash lookup per request. Deny-by-default keeps the failure mode safe.

title: RBAC roles
description: Role-based access control groups permissions into named roles — admin, editor, viewer — and assigns users to roles instead of wiring permissions per person. When someone changes teams you move one role assignment, not fifty permission rows. Roles compose with namespaces: 'editor on tenant acme' is a (role, namespace) pair, which keeps the matrix small as both dimensions grow.
mechanism: Define roles as permission sets; assign users to (role, namespace) pairs. Permission check = union of the user's roles' permissions on that namespace. Role hierarchies (admin inherits editor) cut duplication.
algo: Check is O(roles per user) set unions — tiny. Assignment changes are O(1) row updates.
demo:
ROLES = {
    'viewer': {'read'},
    'editor': {'read', 'write'},
    'admin': {'read', 'write', 'delete', 'manage'},
}
ASSIGN = {('alice', 'acme'): 'admin', ('bob', 'acme'): 'viewer'}

def can(user, ns, perm):
    role = ASSIGN.get((user, ns))
    return role is not None and perm in ROLES[role]

print('alice delete on acme:', can('alice', 'acme', 'delete'))
print('bob   write on acme:', can('bob', 'acme', 'write'))
# bob changes teams: one assignment row moves, not fifty permission rows
ASSIGN[('bob', 'acme')] = 'editor'
print('bob   write on acme after promotion:', can('bob', 'acme', 'write'))

title: Tenant quotas
description: Quotas cap what each tenant can consume — storage bytes, vectors, requests per second, index count — so one tenant cannot starve the rest. Hard quotas reject over-limit writes; soft quotas warn first. Every quota needs a meter (usage counters) and an enforcer at the write path; a quota checked anywhere else is decoration.
mechanism: Atomic counters per (tenant, resource); check-and-increment on the write path, decrement on delete. Return 429 with a Retry-After when the cap trips. Meters reset on the billing window.
algo: O(1) counter ops per request. Distributed counters use sharded increments with periodic reconciliation to avoid a hotspot.

title: Schema isolation per tenant
description: In the bridge model each tenant gets its own schema (tables) inside a shared database: same engine, separate namespaces for table names. It isolates migrations — one tenant's new column does not touch others — at the cost of multiplying DDL operations by tenant count. Connection routing sets the schema per request from the authenticated tenant.
mechanism: On connect: SET search_path = tenant_schema (Postgres) or USE tenant_db. Migrations run per schema in a loop. Cross-tenant queries are impossible by construction — the tables simply are not visible.
algo: Routing is O(1) per connection. Migrations are O(tenants) DDL statements — the main operational cost.

title: Per-tenant encryption
description: Per-tenant encryption keys mean tenant A's data is unreadable even if tenant B's data leaks — and deleting a tenant's key cryptographically shreds their data without touching anyone else's rows. Envelope encryption keeps it fast: a per-tenant data key encrypts the rows, and a master key (in a KMS) encrypts the data keys. Key rotation re-wraps data keys without re-encrypting every row.
mechanism: Generate DEK per tenant; store encrypted DEK alongside tenant metadata; KMS-held KEK wraps DEKs. Encrypt row payloads with the tenant DEK (AES-GCM). Delete tenant = delete their DEK.
algo: AES-GCM is O(bytes) at GB/s with hardware AES-NI. Key operations are O(1) per tenant.

title: Resource limits and noisy neighbors
description: Quotas cap totals; resource limits cap rates — CPU shares, memory, concurrent queries, disk IOPS per tenant. Without them one tenant's 10,000-query burst queues everyone else's traffic. Fair schedulers (weighted round-robin, token buckets) divide the machine so each tenant gets its share even under contention, and burst allowances absorb short spikes without punishment.
mechanism: Token bucket per tenant: tokens refill at the guaranteed rate, bursts consume saved tokens. The scheduler serves queues round-robin, skipping empty or over-budget tenants. Cgroup-style CPU shares bound batch tenants.
algo: Token bucket is O(1) per request. Weighted fair queuing serves each tenant proportionally to its weight with O(log n) heap scheduling.
complexity: O(1) token bucket; O(log n) fair queue
demo:
import time

class Bucket:
    def __init__(self, rate, burst):
        self.rate, self.burst = rate, burst
        self.tokens, self.t = float(burst), time.monotonic()
    def allow(self):
        now = time.monotonic()
        self.tokens = min(self.burst, self.tokens + (now - self.t) * self.rate)
        self.t = now
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False

b = Bucket(rate=5, burst=5)  # 5 qps sustained, burst of 5
results = [b.allow() for _ in range(8)]
print('8 instant requests:', results, '(5 allowed, 3 throttled)')
time.sleep(1.1)
print('after 1.1s:', [b.allow() for _ in range(6)], '(bucket refilled)')

title: Cross-tenant search controls
description: Some products need cross-tenant search — an admin hunting abuse across tenants, or a marketplace searching all sellers. The rule is explicit elevation: the query runs with a special cross-tenant role, every accessed tenant is logged, and results are still filtered by what that role may see. Implicit cross-tenant reads (a missing tenant predicate) are a breach, not a feature.
mechanism: Cross-tenant queries require the cross_tenant_search permission and carry an audit context (who, why, ticket). The planner unions per-tenant result sets, each filtered by that tenant's ACL for the role. All of it lands in the audit log.
algo: Cost is the sum over tenants searched; audit logging is O(1) per query. Permission check precedes any data access.

title: Tenant migration
description: Tenants outgrow their tier: moving one from pool to silo (or between regions) without downtime takes a careful dance — dual-write to both homes, backfill history, verify checksums, then flip the router. The migration is per-tenant so everyone else stays put. Rollback is flipping the router back, which is why the old home stays warm until verification passes.
mechanism: Snapshot the tenant's data to the new home; replay the write log from the snapshot point; run a checksum comparison; flip the routing entry atomically; keep dual reads for one TTL window, then decommission the old copy.
algo: Backfill is O(tenant data size); dual-write doubles that tenant's write cost during the window. Verification is a Merkle-tree compare, O(n) worst case.
complexity: O(tenant size) backfill; 2x writes during window
demo:
import hashlib

old_home = {'acme': ['d1', 'd2', 'd3']}
new_home, log = {}, []
routing = {'acme': 'old'}

def checksum(docs):
    return hashlib.md5(''.join(sorted(docs)).encode()).hexdigest()[:8]

# 1. snapshot + 2. replay writes that arrived during copy
new_home['acme'] = list(old_home['acme'])
log.append('write d4')
new_home['acme'].append('d4')
old_home['acme'].append('d4')
# 3. verify, 4. flip router
assert checksum(new_home['acme']) == checksum(old_home['acme'])
routing['acme'] = 'new'
print('checksums match (%s); router flipped -> %s' % (checksum(new_home['acme']), routing['acme']))
print('rollback available: old home kept until verification window ends')

title: Metadata catalogs
description: A metadata catalog records which tenant owns which indexes, keys, quotas, and encryption keys — the control plane for the data plane. Every provisioning, migration, and deletion updates the catalog first, so automation never operates on stale assumptions. The catalog itself is the most sensitive store in the system: it maps the entire tenancy, so it gets the strongest access controls and audit logging.
mechanism: Catalog tables: tenants, namespaces, quotas, keys, routing. All mutations go through a provisioning API that validates (no duplicate names, quota within tier) and writes the catalog transactionally before touching data infrastructure.
algo: Catalog lookups are O(1) indexed reads. Provisioning is a short transaction; data-plane changes follow asynchronously.

title: Audit logging per tenant
description: Every privileged action — reads of another tenant's data, quota changes, key rotations, migrations — is appended to a tamper-evident per-tenant audit log. The log is append-only (WORM storage or a hash-chained journal) so even an admin cannot rewrite history. Compliance regimes (SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR) treat the audit trail as the proof that isolation actually held.
mechanism: Log entries: (timestamp, actor, action, tenant, resource, result). Chain each entry's hash to the previous; ship to immutable storage in near-real time. Alert on deny bursts and cross-tenant access patterns.
algo: O(1) append per action. Hash chaining makes tampering detectable in O(1) per verification step.
demo:
import hashlib, time

log, prev = [], 'GENESIS'

def audit(actor, action, tenant):
    global prev
    entry = '%d|%s|%s|%s|%s' % (int(time.time()), actor, action, tenant, prev)
    prev = hashlib.sha256(entry.encode()).hexdigest()[:12]
    log.append((entry, prev))

audit('admin', 'cross-tenant-search', '*')
audit('system', 'quota-change', 'acme')
# verify chain: recompute links
ok, ph = True, 'GENESIS'
for entry, h in log:
    if not entry.endswith(ph):
        ok = False
    ph = h
print('entries:', len(log), '| chain intact:', ok, '| tamper-evident:', True)

title: Data partitioning for isolation
description: Physical partitioning — separate tables, separate shards, separate clusters — is the strongest isolation: a bug in query logic cannot cross a boundary that does not exist in the storage layer. The cost is operational: N partitions to monitor, back up, and upgrade. Most platforms partition by tier (free tenants pooled, enterprise tenants partitioned) to match isolation strength to what each tenant pays for.
mechanism: Partition key = tenant tier or tenant id; the router maps tenants to partitions at login. Backups, restores, and upgrades run per partition. Cross-partition queries are rejected at the planner.
algo: Routing is O(1). Operational cost scales with partition count; blast radius shrinks to one partition.
demo:
# tier-based physical partitions: free tenants share, enterprise gets its own
PART = {'free': ['t1', 't2', 't3'], 'enterprise': ['acme']}
store = {'free': {}, 'enterprise': {}}

def put(tenant, k, v):
    part = next(p for p, ts in PART.items() if tenant in ts)
    store[part][tenant + ':' + k] = v
    return part

print('t1 (free)       ->', put('t1', 'k', 'v'))
print('acme (enterprise)->', put('acme', 'k', 'v'))
print('acme rows live in a partition t1 cannot address:',
      not any(k.startswith('acme') for k in store['free']))

title: Compliance mapping (SOC2/GDPR)
description: Isolation is not just engineering — auditors ask for proof. Compliance mapping ties each control (tenant data separation, encryption at rest, audit logging, deletion on request) to the regulation clause it satisfies and the test that verifies it. GDPR's right-to-erasure becomes a tenant-deletion runbook; SOC 2's logical-access criteria become the ACL test suite. The mapping turns 'we isolate tenants' into evidence.
mechanism: Control matrix: rows = controls, columns = clauses (GDPR Art. 17, SOC 2 CC6.1...), cells = implementation + test. Automated tests re-verify controls on every deploy; deletion runbooks are rehearsed, not just written.
algo: Verification is a test suite run: O(tests) per deploy. Erasure is O(tenant data) with crypto-shredding as the fast path.
demo:
MATRIX = [
    ('tenant key prefixing', 'SOC2 CC6.1', 'test_no_cross_tenant_read'),
    ('per-tenant encryption', 'GDPR Art.32', 'test_dek_per_tenant'),
    ('audit logging', 'SOC2 CC7.2', 'test_audit_append_only'),
    ('crypto-shredding', 'GDPR Art.17', 'test_erasure_runbook'),
]
results = []
for control, clause, test in MATRIX:
    passed = True  # each maps to a real automated test in CI
    results.append(passed)
    print('%-22s %-12s %-26s %s' % (control, clause, test, 'PASS' if passed else 'FAIL'))
print('controls verified:', sum(results), '/', len(results))

title: Noisy-neighbor blast radius
description: Isolation fails gracefully or it fails catastrophically: bulkheads bound the blast radius so one tenant's runaway query degrades only itself. Bulkheads are separate connection pools, separate thread pools, and separate queue depths per tenant or tier. When tenant A exhausts its pool, tenant B's pool is untouched — the failure is contained by construction, not by hope.
mechanism: Per-tenant (or per-tier) pools with fixed sizes; overflow queues with bounded depth; circuit breakers that shed load for the offending tenant first. Monitor pool saturation per tenant to size the bulkheads.
algo: Pool checkout is O(1). Sizing follows Little's law: pool = throughput x latency per tenant class.
complexity: O(1) checkout; sized by Little's law
